title: The Witnesses Disagreed About the Jacket
subtitle: Character stories, dialogue and consequential choices

opening.title: My Summit Had Two Eyewitnesses and Neither Endorsed Me
paragraphs: By the time we reached the final wording, the casino convention floor contained a working signing table, an actual clear aisle and a portrait of me big enough to possess its own weather. Nigga, peace had acquired infrastructure.
Mika stood beneath the portrait with a tape measure. They said it might have to leave through the loading entrance. I said that was no way to treat the face of reconciliation.
'It's the width of reconciliation,' Mika replied.
Shawna touched my arm. 'Baby, stop negotiating with the tape.'
At the good table, Rae had put a small wedge under the troublesome leg. Nia watched her check it, put the tools away and return to the draft. My wife caught me watching Nia watch Rae.
'Leave it alone,' she whispered. 'I was observing a promising alliance.' 'They can flirt without a ribbon cutting.'

Across the room sat the women whose memories had helped turn my game night into The Second Great Butch vs. Stud War. Auntie June, eighty-two, retired bus driver and proud butch, had commandeered the chair with the best view of the music. Odessa, known as Dez, eighty-four, retired seamstress and equally proud stud, sat beside her holding the disputed jacket.
They agreed the trouble began at the Blue Comet Social Club in 1967. They disagreed about the song, the weather, the jacket's destination and whether June had ever said she was sorry.
'I said it was unfortunate,' June told Nia.
'That the jukebox broke,' Dez said. 'You didn't mean my coat.'
I offered to appoint a historical commission. June looked at me. 'You got biscuits?'
Rosa brought biscuits before I could explain the commission's mandate. Tank followed with tea. My brother had identified which contribution would receive the more favourable account.
The original peace agreement was supposedly unsigned. June said someone lost the pen. Dez said the pen went home in June's pocket. June said a good crossword was not going to complete itself.
Nia asked what they wanted settled tonight. Dez could return June's jacket, then borrow it again by asking. Everybody could choose a jukebox song. The old stories did not have to become identical.
'And nobody makes me play something because they bought it,' Dez added.
'That sentence belongs in there,' Rae said.
I looked toward the portrait. Its expression suggested generosity without limits. Its invoice suggested limits should have arrived considerably earlier.

Velvet Payroll crossed the floor in half her costume, carrying the other half like an expensive weather event. She wanted her show time confirmed. Remy, currently becoming King Receipts, wanted the working microphone and a place for the ridiculous fanfare he had defended through four separate departments.

Kit, a white butch with excellent opinions about her own entrance, wanted to sing under the light she had chosen. Mercedes wanted her arrangement heard. Porsche wanted one photograph everybody actually agreed to stand in. None of these wishes required another summit about what sort of person had permission to want them.
Nia put her name beside both caucuses she belonged to and carried on correcting the last sentence. Rae passed her a cup. The room survived this overlap without installing a second Nia.
I said I was delighted by the complexity of our coalition.
'Nigga, drink your tea,' Velvet told me.
Rae asked Nia whether the pen always made her writing look like that. Nia admitted the pen was innocent. Rae turned the draft sideways, smiling. 'I can learn it.'
Something quiet happened between them. Not mysterious. Two adults taking pleasure in the particular person across the table.
I almost called the photographer.
Shawna closed my hand around my cup instead. 'You can witness something without owning the picture.'
June asked Dez which song she intended to choose. Dez said it would be a surprise. June declared surprises responsible for at least half the original war.
Mika dimmed the portrait's lamp to improve the table light. My enormous forehead disappeared from the ceiling. The actual people became easier to see.
I sat beside my wife, accepted a biscuit and opened the next story.
The room had enough narrators. For a little while, I intended to hear some of them.

games.title: Coffee Talk
games.case_title: The Barista Declined My Peace Prize
scene: Coffee Talk put a late-night café on the screen. I put six empty cups in front of Rae and announced that refreshments would heal the remaining divisions.
'Where's the coffee?' she asked. 'Arriving as a concept.' 'Nigga, I repair bikes. I know when a thing has no fuel.'
Nia brought her a real cup. No speech. Just remembered how Rae had ordered it earlier, which struck me as suspiciously effective diplomacy.
I offered to name their emerging relationship after the summit. Nia kept looking at Rae. 'Would you like to sit beside me?'
Rae moved her chair. I was still holding the cups. Tank took two and used them to collect the crackers falling through my decorative snack basket.
The café customers had their own reasons for talking. So did the women beside me. Rae wanted to hear about Nia's ridiculous first job; Nia wanted a second coffee to last longer than the first.
I supplied both drinks. Shawna kissed my cheek. Finally, a service contract with benefits.

games.title: Coffee Talk Episode 2: Hibiscus & Butterfly
games.case_title: The Butterfly Had a Catering Budget
scene: The returning café in Hibiscus & Butterfly made Mika propose a signature drink for the summit. I approved before asking what signature meant. An expensive habit, beautifully consistent.
Velvet Payroll wanted a butterfly in the foam. Rae wanted coffee that still tasted like coffee. Nia drew something on a napkin to explain a compromise.
'That's a butterfly?' I asked. 'That's my name,' Nia said. 'You asked me to sign the sample order.'
Kit found her reading glasses on top of the sugar and examined the napkin. 'I can confirm several intentions. None of them are letters.'
Rae laughed, then folded the napkin into her pocket. Nia watched it disappear with the pleased surprise of somebody whose bad handwriting had finally secured a useful outcome.
I asked whether we could enlarge it above the stage. Velvet slid the printing quote back toward me. 'Nigga, let one small thing be small.'
The drinks arrived without edible portraits. Everybody finished theirs. My proposed foam monument remained entirely theoretical.

games.title: VA-11 Hall-A: Cyberpunk Bartender Action
games.case_title: My Cocktail Had No Constituency
scene: The cyberpunk bar in VA-11 Hall-A encouraged me to invent a drink called Executive Intimacy. Shawna asked what went in it. I said expensive things served close together.
'That's the seating plan,' she said. 'Try again.'
Velvet wanted her usual drink before rehearsal, not a beverage bearing the emotional difficulties of the host. Remy wanted water. His victory fanfare involved a note he had never previously met.
I treated these as negotiating positions and began describing a glittering pitcher. Rae took the menu from my hand. 'Nigga, people already told you what they want.'
Nia ordered something for herself. Rae ordered something different. They touched glasses without establishing a joint beverage policy, a development I found administratively reckless.
The fictional customers brought their problems to a counter. Ours brought actual orders. Porsche wrote them down and handed them to the waiter before I could announce a tasting committee.
Shawna kept Executive Intimacy as a private joke. She said we could discuss the seating later.

games.title: The Red Strings Club
games.case_title: The Emotional Sculpture Looked Like My Ear
scene: The Red Strings Club raised questions about shaping other people's feelings. I immediately offered the summit a sculpture intended to inspire unanimous affection for its host.
Mika rotated the clay model. 'It looks like an ear.' 'That represents listening.' 'Why is the ear wearing your watch?'
Velvet wanted a stage entrance, not an emotional adjustment. She moved the model away from the lighting diagram and asked Remy to test the microphone she actually needed.
Nia said she could draft a clause about requests. I told her my sculpture communicated without words. Rae leaned closer. 'It's communicating that you bought clay before sandwiches.'
That hurt because the sandwiches were late.
I tried squeezing the clay into a heart. It became a second ear. Tank placed the two together and said the summit finally had enough equipment to hear Rosa asking for plates.
The game could keep its difficult questions about influence. I fetched plates. Velvet thanked the technician, not my sculpture, when the microphone worked.

games.title: Neo Cab
games.case_title: The Passenger Rated My Marriage Advice
scene: Neo Cab's passengers made me offer Rae an imaginary ride across the convention floor. I rolled up in a chair, opened a nonexistent door and asked where she wanted to go.
'To the woman holding two coffees,' she said. 'Excellent. Before we arrive, a few thoughts about relationships.' 'Cancel the trip.'
Nia was only three tables away. My proposed service had already introduced a delay, a fare dispute and an unsolicited emotional assessment.
Shawna stopped the chair with one hand. 'Baby, you could just move your foot.'
I moved it. Rae walked past me, sat beside Nia and immediately received the second coffee. No application required.
The driver's relationships and money on screen still interested them. Rae asked Nia which passenger she would find hardest to hear out. Nia looked toward me, smiling into her cup.
'Aiden gets four stars,' she said. I straightened. 'Out of how many?'
Tank started laughing before she answered. That nigga had learned to recognise a meter running.

games.case_title: The Listening Service Wanted a Tip
scene: Eliza's scripted support gave me an idea for improving summit hospitality. I stood beside the buffet and told Kit I understood her concern before she had expressed one.
'Where are my glasses?' she asked. 'Your feelings are valid.' 'My glasses are missing.'
I nodded with expensive sincerity. She reached past my shoulder and took them from the pocket where I had put them while demonstrating attentive listening.
Nia nearly spilled her tea. Rae passed her a napkin before I could describe the incident as a breakthrough.

Kit wanted to pick her karaoke song. She had not requested a journey through my capacity for empathy. Once she could read the list, she chose something loud enough to punish an indifferent microphone.
Mercedes asked whether Kit wanted accompaniment. 'Yes. And no announcement that I am brave.'
The story on screen could investigate the difference between listening and performing concern. Mine had developed a practical test: Kit began singing, and I remained quiet.
Shawna tipped me with half her dessert for maintaining the new service.

games.title: Citizen Sleeper
games.case_title: The Dice Refused to Sponsor My Portrait
scene: Citizen Sleeper's scarce resources made the remaining summit budget look less like a number and more like several people waiting for dinner. I proposed solving this with confidence.
Rae counted the available dessert portions. Nia counted the guests. Tank counted again because he disliked the first answer.
'We could cut my portrait lighting,' I said generously. Shawna checked the bill. 'That has its own battery.' 'Nigga, I invested in resilience.'
Mika suggested moving the spare flowers and using their table for additional plates. Velvet offered to shorten her costume reveal if it got the cooks another clear path.
Everybody was finding something useful to give. I had contributed an illuminated explanation of why my contribution was difficult.
The daily choices on screen carried needs that could not all disappear through enthusiasm. I paid for the extra desserts.
Rae saved Nia a seat and half a tart. Nia split it unevenly in Rae's favour. Tank watched this resource allocation with professional respect.

games.title: Citizen Sleeper 2: Starward Vector
games.case_title: The Crew Declined My Inspirational Luggage
scene: Citizen Sleeper 2 put an uncertain crew journey before us. I decided our signing team needed a name, matching bags and a statement about carrying each other.
Remy held up the bag I had ordered. Its handle came off. 'Are we starting with the metaphor broken?'
Mika wanted the spare cable inside it. Velvet wanted the cash envelope for the performers. Rae wanted the table stabiliser we had somehow packed beneath my commemorative slippers.
I said all missions suffered unexpected stress. Nia examined the slippers. 'Some stress arrives with a monogram.'
The game's imperfect dice and contracts gave everybody enough genuine uncertainty to discuss. Our own crew did not need an additional challenge locating equipment in my personality.
Tank tipped the bag gently onto the sofa. Everything appeared at once. Rae fixed the table leg; Remy connected the microphone; Velvet counted her envelope and grinned.
I wore the slippers. Shawna called them excellent for the short voyage between the sofa and whatever useful thing she asked me to fetch.

games.title: Disco Elysium - The Final Cut
games.case_title: My Inner Voices Lost the Microphone
scene: Disco Elysium's competing inner voices made me feel represented. One part of me wanted the summit to finish. Another wanted my closing entrance accompanied by thunder.
'Which part ordered the smoke?' Shawna asked. 'Artistic judgment.' 'The hotel calls it a cleaning surcharge.'
Velvet said the smoke belonged to her number, which she had actually rehearsed. Remy backed her until he remembered his own fanfare needed the same technician.
Nia asked whether either performance needed to precede the final wording. Both performers said no. My thunder suddenly had no surviving relative.
Rae borrowed Kit's glasses to read a small line. Kit said she could borrow them only if somebody remembered where they went. I announced that a detective was among them.
'Find the pen you're holding, nigga,' Tank said.
The game offered a rich investigation. Our immediate mystery solved itself when I lowered my hand. Nia took the pen, read the disputed sentence aloud and left my weather system out of it.

Rae described the little lunch counter by her shop. Nia wanted to visit. Rae said Thursdays had the good soup and the least theatrical customers.
I offered to arrange a limousine. 'You can recommend a soup without acquiring transport,' Shawna told me.
Porsche unhooked one side of the backdrop so the carts could pass. My enormous eye folded neatly against a palm tree.

games.case_title: The Route Went Through My Introduction
scene: Kentucky Route Zero's strange working journey inspired Mika to describe our evening as a passage through temporary architecture. I thought that sounded expensive enough to approve.
Then a waiter asked which door reached the kitchen. Mika pointed at the floor plan. The waiter pointed at the actual wall.
'That door exists in the earlier drawing,' Mika said. 'My tray exists now,' the waiter replied.
Rae moved a folding screen. An ordinary door emerged behind it. I announced a discovery. 'Nigga, it has EXIT written over it,' Tank said.
Nia liked how the game left space around what people meant. She asked Rae about the longest ride she had ever taken without a particular destination.
Rae told her. I tried to improve the story by adding a helicopter. Shawna squeezed my hand with the exact pressure required to land it.
The waiter returned with dinner. Mika abandoned the drawing, kept the beautiful lighting and opened the route that actually went somewhere. Our strange journey had found the potatoes.

games.title: Night in the Woods
games.case_title: The Homecoming Band Had Already Replaced Me
scene: Night in the Woods brought old friendships and a changing hometown into the room. Kit remembered the terrible band she had joined in her twenties.
'What did you play?' Remy asked. 'Bass. What did you play?' 'A duke once. Reviews were divided.'
June remembered the Blue Comet band playing it in 1967. Dez said there had been a jukebox, not a band. 'It sounded live,' June insisted. 'So did you,' Dez replied.
I offered to join their reunion. Kit asked what instrument I played. I said atmosphere. 'We already had a broken amplifier,' she replied.
Rae leaned against Nia's chair and listened. Nia kept time with her pen, producing a tiny rhythm and three additional dots on the final wording.

The game's active movement still needed its own trial. The music in our room needed no intervention from me. Velvet took the chorus, Kit laughed through a forgotten bridge, and even the waiter waited.
I supplied the last note by dropping a spoon. Nobody invited it back.

Rae opened it. A tiny service balcony contained two stacked chairs and a mop. Nia looked at me with professional interest.
'Exclusive,' Tank said. 'Nobody else wants it.'
Velvet took one chair, sat beside the open door and announced she would perform a tragic monologue about misleading adjectives. Remy supplied a mournful chord from his phone.
The game's psychological horror could reshape what a claim meant. My claim needed only an ordinary door to become considerably less impressive.
Shawna pulled me toward the real window overlooking the city. 'This is enough,' she said.
I agreed before narrating anything else. Behind us, Velvet's princess demanded a better balcony and received a standing ovation from the mop.

scene: Scarlet Hollow's troubled town and branching relationships made Rae ask whether the summit would look different through each guest's account. I said mine would be definitive.
Nia placed the final wording in front of me. There was a greasy thumbprint over the word voluntary.
'That's an editorial mark,' I said. 'That's a samosa,' Rosa replied.
Kit read the clean copy. Velvet checked her show time. Remy checked that his name still contained Receipts. Everybody found the part they needed without pretending to have written the whole evening.
The game's unfinished release remained an unfinished release; nobody in our room could promise its ending. We could finish this particular draft.
Nia asked whether Rae wanted any change. Rae said the signing table was level and the snack clause was understandable. 'The dance invitation stands?' Nia asked.

I lifted my clean hands away from the paper. Shawna smiled. Final wording agreed, portrait reimbursement still absent, and two women waiting for the song after the signatures.

interludes.title: The Dance Was Not a Reward for Being Useful
paragraphs: Nia's invitation reached Rae just as Kit asked whether Rae could fix the little light above the karaoke screen. Rae had spent most of the evening making objects less likely to collapse. She put the note down without reading it and reached for her tools.
Nia covered the tool bag with her hand.
'You can say no,' she said.
Kit looked from one woman to the other. 'I asked. I didn't issue an order.'
'Then let her answer before you tell the technician she's coming.'
The technician stood behind Kit holding a ladder. Nigga, witnesses had developed terrible timing.
I offered to buy another light. All three women ignored me with impressive coordination.
Rae took her hand off the bag. 'I don't want to climb anything. I want to read this note.'

Kit turned to the technician. 'I'm sorry. I assumed.' He nodded and carried the ladder toward the lamp. Kit watched him go. 'We already had this argument over the fees. Apparently I can understand a budget faster than I can stop doing it.'
The less practical problem stayed.
'You could have told me,' Kit said.
'I just did.'
Nia moved her hand away. Rae did not pick up the tools.

Kit was white, butch, wearing a carefully chosen suit and the expression of somebody discovering that a useful intention had arrived badly. Rae was a Black stud with a mechanic's hands and several very specific reasons to dislike being treated as the room's available solution.
I had printed their labels across opposite sides of a banner. It looked impressive from the lift. Up close it had done a remarkably poor job of explaining either woman.
'When I walk into a room like this,' Kit said, 'I already feel as though people are waiting for me to prove I can be useful. I thought we were doing the same thing.'
'We can recognise something without having the same night,' Rae replied.
Kit folded her arms, caught herself and let them drop. 'I know that.'
'You might. You still sent the ladder.'
Velvet sat on the edge of the table. She had heard enough to stop arranging her entrance and start listening.
Kit looked at Rae's tool bag. 'I liked that you seemed certain. You knew what to do with the table. I was still trying to ask for the right light without apologising for having a face.'
'You thought certainty meant I wasn't tired.'
'Maybe.'

Rae looked at the note beneath her hand. 'Sometimes I like fixing things. Sometimes I like being good at something in front of a woman I want. Both can be true, and I can still want the next person to leave the screwdriver alone.'
Nia smiled, but only briefly.
'You don't have to earn this chair,' she said.
Rae turned toward her. 'I know.'
'Do you?'
The room got quiet enough for my portrait's ventilation fan to sound obscene.
I reached for its switch. Shawna pointed to the correct one before I blacked out the entire floor.

Nia waited until the fan stopped. 'I like the way you look at me. I like your terrible opinions about the biscuits. I wanted to flirt with you. Then every time something happened, I became the person who could make your answer sound diplomatic.'
'I didn't ask you to do that,' Rae said.
'No. I did it. I'm stopping.'
She put the marked-up draft on the table. The gesture was small. Rae watched it as though Nia had moved a wall.

'I'm Black, trans, a lesbian, a femme and a lawyer,' Nia said. 'Tonight you have all managed to remember the lawyer whenever a sentence becomes awkward. I would like the woman in the nice dress to get a turn.'
Velvet lifted her glass. 'The dress has been waiting patiently.'
Nia laughed. Rae did not reach for a polished reply.
'I don't want you to translate me,' she said. 'I want you to tell me when I'm being an ass. Preferably before it becomes a programme item.'
'You're being an ass about accepting help.'
'Excellent. Efficient. No billable preamble.'
Kit sat, leaving room between their chairs instead of turning the whole exchange into a panel.
'I don't want the banner to decide what I can ask you,' she said. 'But I can see I've been using same side when I meant please recognise me.'
Rae nodded. 'Ask for that. Don't send equipment.'
June arrived with tea and looked at the banner. 'White butches over here, Black studs over there. Where did you intend to put my Black butch ass?'
I began to explain visual balance.
'Try the chair,' June said, and sat wherever she pleased.
Dez followed. She put the borrowed jacket over June's chair and took the cup June offered her. The banner had lost another jurisdiction.
Kit looked at June. 'I grew up thinking there was one way to look like I belonged. Then I spent years resenting people who looked at ease in it.'
'Who looked at ease?' June asked.
Kit laughed despite herself. 'Fair.'

'I like being butch,' Kit continued. 'I like how my shoulders sit in this jacket. I like a woman calling me handsome without sounding surprised by her own taste. I don't want to speak about all of it as damage.'
'Good,' Rae said. 'Because the jacket looks good. I noticed before we argued.'
Kit looked pleased, then slightly embarrassed by how pleased. Nia told her to enjoy the compliment without preparing a counterstatement.
Rae rubbed one hand over her knee. 'Stud is my word. It doesn't mean I'm volunteering to be a man in somebody else's romance. It doesn't mean I don't want tenderness because I like this shirt.'
Nia touched the cuff, waiting until Rae turned her hand toward hers.
'I like this shirt too,' she said. 'I also like when you stop arranging the space around me long enough to ask where I want to stand.'
'I was trying to make a path.'
'I know. Sometimes I want the path. Sometimes I want your hand. They're different requests.'
I felt Shawna glance at me. Nigga, a lesson had crossed the room without my name appearing anywhere in it.
Remy came over carrying the working microphone. He had missed the start, asked what was happening and accepted Kit's short answer instead of inventing one.
'My gay friends sometimes introduce me as the one who understands women,' he said. 'I'm a man with one particular history. I'm not a customer-service desk for everybody they date.'
Velvet nodded. 'And I put on a queen because I want this room watching the number I rehearsed. That doesn't entitle anybody to invent the rest of my life from the costume.'
'They do enjoy a convenient character,' Kit said.
'So do I,' Velvet replied. 'Mine charges.'

The joke loosened something without ending the conversation. Kit asked Rae whether she wanted another coffee. Rae said water. Kit brought water and did not make the correction into a test of her goodness.
Nia finally picked up the note. 'Now can somebody tell me whether this invitation is legible?'
Rae read it sideways. 'Are you asking me to dance or to inspect a second table?'
'Dance.'
'Then ask.'
'Will you dance with me after the signing?'
'Yes. And if I'm nervous, don't let me pretend I need to check the furniture.'
Nia smiled fully. 'If I'm nervous, don't let me turn it into a contract.'
'You can both be nervous,' Shawna said. 'The floor will cope.'
Rae looked at Nia's hand. 'When we get there, will you hold me first? I keep reaching like I'm supposed to know the whole way.'
'I'd like that,' Nia said. She offered her hand, palm up. Rae took it. Nothing about her shirt, her name or her chosen word needed altering for the gesture to fit.
I offered to have the floor inspected. Shawna put one finger against my lips.
Mercedes asked what song they wanted. They chose together. Kit wanted her own song afterwards; Velvet wanted the time she had booked; Remy wanted his ridiculous fanfare to survive being funny.
Nobody's desire dissolved into the couple's. The room held several wants at once, untidily, without arranging them into opposing armies.
Rae folded the note and kept it. Nia asked why. 'Because you made a bad drawing of a good question,' Rae said.
'That's my handwriting.'
'I know. I'm learning it.'

I looked at the banner again. Its enormous words could still sell a theatrical war. They could not do this part: two women admitting what the pose concealed, another recognising what she had assumed, and June refusing to move to make my categories prettier.
I asked Mika to lower it before the music. Mika asked where to put it.
Shawna pointed at my portrait's transport crate. 'Plenty of room for another oversized explanation.'
Nigga, I held the crate open myself.

ending.title: The Final Wording Left My Face Out of It
paragraphs: Nia read the finished wording once, slowly enough for everybody to follow. No heroic music beneath it. Remy had offered, but even he agreed that a fanfare could make a sentence about borrowing coats sound like a siege.

People could choose a game, ask for help, watch, take a break or decline. Sharing a controller required an actual agreement about who did what. The jukebox belonged to everyone's choices. Borrowing the old jacket began with asking the person who currently had it.
My portrait appeared nowhere.
I cleared my throat.
Shawna looked at me. 'You signed that order yourself.'
'I haven't raised the matter.'
'You raised your reimbursement throat.'
Rae laughed. Nia waited until the room settled, then asked whether the wording described what we had actually agreed.
June wanted it clear that she could still say Dez remembered the weather wrong. Dez wanted it clear that she could still point out the jacket's excellent lining.
'You can both keep telling your stories,' Nia said. 'This settles tonight's arrangements.'
They approved. The old war did not need a winner to stop acquiring new invoices.

Velvet checked that her paid performance stayed paid regardless of whether everybody watched. Remy checked his cue. Kit asked for the lamp to remain where she could read the song list. Mika checked the clock and looked briefly overcome by the astonishing possibility that the gala might begin.
Rosa brought the last tray past the table without catching her sleeve. Rae's repaired leg stayed steady. Tank sat beside her and declared the engineering department a success.
Nia put down the pen. Rae took her hand under the edge of the table. I saw their shoulders relax at the same time.
'Still after the signatures?' Rae asked.
'Still,' Nia said.
I wanted to tell them that a great romance deserved an audience. Then I remembered several great romantic moments in my own marriage had occurred specifically because the audience left.
Shawna caught my eye. The woman could follow a terrible idea across my face before I found words expensive enough to decorate it.
'Good choice, baby,' she said.
'You don't know what I chose.'
'I know what you didn't say.'

The clean draft went into its folder. June and Dez rose slowly, helping each other without deciding which assistance counted toward the coat account. They would return for the signing after the last shared-play trial.
Mercedes touched the first chord of the chosen dance song. Rae looked toward the floor; Nia watched Rae.
Mika asked whether my portrait's lamp could stay off for the rest of the evening.
I looked at the faces already lit around the table.
'Yeah,' I said. 'Leave it.'
Nigga, the final wording was agreed. Nobody had surrendered a name, a story or the right to go home. I had surrendered one unnecessary spotlight, which felt like enough personal history for tonight.
